q: What is the origin of gluteus maximus?
o: Posterior ilium, sacrum, coccyx and sacrotuberous ligament
e: It arises broadly from the posterior ilium behind the posterior gluteal line, the sacrum, coccyx and sacrotuberous ligament, and inserts on the iliotibial band and the gluteal tuberosity of the femur.

q: Gluteus maximus performs which primary actions?
e: Hip extension and external rotation, with the upper fibres also assisting abduction. It is the prime mover for standing up from a squat and for driving the hip forward.

q: Where does gluteus medius insert?
o: Lateral surface of the greater trochanter
e: It runs from the outer surface of the ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines to the lateral greater trochanter, which is why it abducts and stabilises the pelvis.

q: What is the main functional role of gluteus medius during single-leg stance?
o: Flexing the hip to swing the leg
Preventing the opposite side of the pelvis from dropping
e: It stabilises the pelvis in the frontal plane. Weakness produces a Trendelenburg sign, the contralateral pelvis dropping, and contributes to knee valgus in a squat.

q: The anterior fibres of gluteus medius and minimus produce which rotation?
e: Anterior fibres internally rotate the hip, posterior fibres externally rotate it. Gluteus minimus lies deep to medius and shares its abduction role.

q: Tensor fasciae latae inserts into which structure?
e: TFL runs from the anterior superior iliac spine into the iliotibial band, which continues to Gerdy's tubercle on the tibia. It flexes, abducts and internally rotates the hip.

q: Which two muscles combine to form iliopsoas?
e: Psoas major arises from the bodies and transverse processes of T12 to L5; iliacus from the iliac fossa. They share an insertion on the lesser trochanter of the femur.

q: Where does iliopsoas insert?
e: The lesser trochanter, on the medial femur. That line of pull makes it the strongest hip flexor and gives it an influence on the lumbar spine.

q: Why does a tight psoas affect the lumbar spine?
o: It originates on the lumbar vertebrae, so shortening tilts the pelvis anteriorly and increases lordosis
It shares a tendon with erector spinae
e: Psoas major spans from the lumbar vertebrae to the femur. Prolonged sitting shortens it, and standing then pulls the pelvis and lower back forward, the LPHC distortion pattern.

q: Which muscle is the longest in the human body?
e: Sartorius runs from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial tibia at the pes anserinus. It flexes, abducts and externally rotates the hip and flexes the knee, the cross-legged sitting position.

q: Piriformis performs which action with the hip extended?
e: It runs from the anterior sacrum to the greater trochanter and externally rotates the extended hip. With the hip flexed beyond about 90 degrees its line of pull changes and it abducts.

q: Which muscle group is the antagonist to the hip adductors?
o: Gluteus medius and minimus with TFL
e: The abductors oppose the adductors in the frontal plane. Overactive adductors with weak outer hip is the pattern behind knees buckling inward in an overhead squat.

q: Where does the adductor group originate?
o: The pubis and, for adductor magnus, also the ischial tuberosity
e: Adductor longus, brevis and magnus, pectineus and gracilis arise from the pubic region. The posterior head of adductor magnus also arises from the ischial tuberosity, which gives it a hamstring-like extension action.

q: Where do most of the adductors insert?
o: The linea aspera of the femur
e: The linea aspera, the ridge on the posterior femur. Gracilis is the exception: it crosses the knee to the medial tibia, so it also flexes the knee.

q: Which adductor also assists hip extension?
o: Adductor magnus, through its posterior head
e: The posterior or hamstring part of adductor magnus arises from the ischial tuberosity and inserts on the adductor tubercle, giving it a powerful extension action alongside adduction.

q: Which adductor crosses two joints?
e: Gracilis runs from the pubis to the medial tibia at the pes anserinus, crossing both hip and knee. It adducts the hip and assists knee flexion and internal rotation.

q: Which of the four quadriceps crosses the hip joint as well as the knee?
e: Rectus femoris arises from the anterior inferior iliac spine, so it flexes the hip as well as extending the knee. The three vasti arise from the femur and only extend the knee.

q: Where do all four quadriceps insert?
o: Via the quadriceps tendon into the patella, then the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity
e: They converge on the patella, which acts as a sesamoid bone increasing the lever arm, and the patellar ligament carries the force to the tibial tuberosity.

q: Why is rectus femoris weakened as a knee extensor when the hip is already flexed?
o: Active insufficiency: it is already shortened at the hip, so it cannot shorten much further at the knee
e: A two-joint muscle shortened at one end cannot produce full force at the other. That is why seated leg extension emphasises the vasti and a hip-extended position favours rectus femoris.

q: Which vastus is most associated with patellar tracking on the medial side?
o: Vastus medialis, particularly the oblique fibres
e: Vastus medialis, and specifically the vastus medialis obliquus, counters the lateral pull of vastus lateralis and helps keep the patella tracking centrally.

q: Which three muscles make up the hamstring group?
e: Biceps femoris sits laterally with two heads; semitendinosus and semimembranosus sit medially. All but the short head of biceps femoris cross both hip and knee.

q: Where do the hamstrings originate?
o: The ischial tuberosity, except the short head of biceps femoris
e: The ischial tuberosity is the common origin. The short head of biceps femoris arises from the linea aspera of the femur instead, so it crosses only the knee.

q: Where does biceps femoris insert?
e: The fibular head, laterally. Semitendinosus inserts on the medial tibia at the pes anserinus and semimembranosus on the posterior medial tibial condyle.

q: What are the two main actions of the hamstrings?
o: Hip adduction and ankle plantar flexion
e: They extend the hip and flex the knee. Because they cross two joints they also decelerate knee extension eccentrically, which is where sprinting strains occur.

q: Which hamstring rotates the flexed knee externally?
o: None of them rotate the knee
e: Biceps femoris is lateral, so it externally rotates the flexed knee. The two medial hamstrings, semitendinosus and semimembranosus, internally rotate it.

q: In a squat, what is the hamstrings' role in NASM's terms?
o: Synergist to the gluteus maximus, and a knee stabiliser
e: Gluteus maximus and quadriceps are the agonists; the hamstrings assist hip extension as synergists while helping stabilise the knee against anterior shear.

q: Which small muscle unlocks the fully extended knee?
e: Popliteus runs from the lateral femoral condyle to the posterior tibia and internally rotates the tibia on the femur, unlocking the screw-home mechanism so flexion can begin.

q: Where does gastrocnemius originate?
o: The femoral condyles, above the knee
e: Two heads from the medial and lateral femoral condyles, so it crosses the knee as well as the ankle. It therefore both plantarflexes the ankle and assists knee flexion.

q: What distinguishes soleus from gastrocnemius?
o: Soleus crosses the knee, gastrocnemius does not
Soleus originates below the knee on the tibia and fibula, so it does not cross the knee
e: Because soleus does not cross the knee it plantarflexes regardless of knee angle, which is why a bent-knee calf raise targets it while a straight-leg raise favours gastrocnemius.

q: Gastrocnemius and soleus insert via which structure?
o: The Achilles tendon, onto the calcaneus
e: The Achilles, or calcaneal, tendon is the thickest and strongest tendon in the body, and both muscles are collectively called triceps surae.

q: What is the origin and insertion of tibialis anterior?
o: Lateral tibia to the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal
e: From the lateral surface of the tibia, crossing the front of the ankle to the medial cuneiform and base of the first metatarsal. It dorsiflexes and inverts the foot.

q: Tibialis anterior is the antagonist to which muscles?
e: It dorsiflexes against their plantar flexion. In the lower-extremity distortion pattern the calves are stretched and the anterior tibialis is strengthened as a foot and ankle stabiliser.

q: Which muscle supports the medial longitudinal arch from behind?
e: Tibialis posterior runs from the posterior tibia and fibula, behind the medial malleolus, to the navicular and other tarsals. It plantarflexes and inverts and is a key arch support.

q: What do the peroneal, or fibular, muscles do?
o: Evert the foot and assist plantar flexion
e: Peroneus longus and brevis run down the lateral fibula behind the lateral malleolus. They evert the foot and resist excessive inversion, protecting against ankle sprains.

q: Where does rectus abdominis attach?
o: Pubic crest and symphysis to the fifth to seventh costal cartilages and xiphoid process
e: It runs vertically from pubis to lower ribs and sternum, so it flexes the trunk in the sagittal plane and posteriorly tilts the pelvis.

q: Which abdominal muscle runs horizontally and acts like a corset?
e: Transversus abdominis is the deepest layer, with fibres running horizontally from the thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest and lower ribs to the linea alba. It compresses the abdomen and stabilises the spine.

q: Which way do the external oblique fibres run?
o: Downward and forward, like hands into front pockets
e: External oblique fibres run inferomedially, hands-into-pockets. Internal oblique fibres run perpendicular to them, upward and forward.

q: Trunk rotation to the left uses which combination?
o: Left external oblique and right internal oblique
Right external oblique and left internal oblique
e: The external oblique rotates the trunk to the opposite side, the internal oblique to the same side. So left rotation pairs the right external with the left internal.

q: Which muscle stabilises the spine segment by segment and is a key deep stabiliser?
e: Multifidus spans from the sacrum and transverse processes to the spinous processes two to four levels above, controlling intersegmental motion. It works with transversus abdominis in the deep core.

q: Quadratus lumborum runs between which structures?
o: Iliac crest and the twelfth rib and lumbar transverse processes
e: It laterally flexes the trunk, elevates the hip, and stabilises the twelfth rib during breathing. Unilateral tightness contributes to a hip hike and pelvic asymmetry.

q: Which three columns make up erector spinae, from lateral to medial?
e: Iliocostalis is most lateral, longissimus in the middle, spinalis closest to the spinous processes. Together they extend the spine and, unilaterally, laterally flex and rotate it.

q: What is the antagonist to erector spinae in the sagittal plane?
e: Erector spinae extends the trunk, rectus abdominis flexes it. Their balance, along with the hip flexors and gluteals, determines pelvic tilt.

q: What is the diaphragm's origin and insertion?
o: Lumbar vertebrae, lower ribs and xiphoid process, converging on a central tendon
e: It attaches around the lower thoracic outlet and converges on a central tendon. Contraction flattens the dome, increasing thoracic volume, which is the primary mechanism of inspiration.

q: Where does latissimus dorsi originate?
o: Thoracolumbar fascia, spinous processes of T7 down, iliac crest and lower ribs
e: It has a broad origin across the lower back and inserts into the intertubercular groove of the humerus, which is why it links the arm to the pelvis and lumbar spine.

q: What are the primary actions of latissimus dorsi?
o: Shoulder flexion, abduction and external rotation
Shoulder extension, adduction and internal rotation
e: Extension, adduction and internal rotation of the humerus. It is the agonist in a row and a pull-up, with the biceps as a synergist.

q: Which muscle is the antagonist to latissimus dorsi in an overhead press?
o: Latissimus dorsi is itself the antagonist to the deltoid in an overhead press
e: In NASM's table for the overhead press the deltoid is the agonist, triceps the synergist, rotator cuff the stabiliser and latissimus dorsi the antagonist, because it pulls the arm back down.

q: Where do the rhomboids attach?
o: Spinous processes of C7 to T5 to the medial border of the scapula
e: Rhomboid minor above, major below. They retract the scapulae and rotate them downward, and they are strengthened in the upper-extremity distortion pattern.

q: What does levator scapulae do, and where does it attach?
o: Depresses the scapula; from the ribs
Elevates the scapula; from the transverse processes of C1 to C4 to the superior medial scapula
Protracts the scapula; from the sternum
Retracts the scapula; from the thoracic spine
e: It elevates the scapula and rotates it downward, and it laterally flexes the neck. Chronically tight in forward-head, rounded-shoulder posture.

q: The three portions of trapezius do different things. Which is correct?
o: Upper depresses, middle protracts, lower elevates
Upper elevates, middle retracts, lower depresses
Upper retracts, middle elevates, lower protracts
e: Upper fibres elevate the scapula and extend the neck, middle fibres retract, lower fibres depress. Upper and lower together produce upward rotation, needed for overhead reaching.

q: In the upper-extremity distortion pattern, which parts of trapezius are stretched and which strengthened?
o: Stretch the middle and lower, strengthen the upper
Stretch the upper, strengthen the middle and lower
e: Upper trapezius is overactive and gets flexibility work; middle and lower trapezius, along with the rhomboids and rotator cuff, are underactive and get strengthening.

q: Which muscle protracts the scapula and holds it flat against the rib cage?
e: Serratus anterior runs from the outer surfaces of ribs 1 to 8 or 9 to the medial border of the scapula. Weakness produces winging, and it also upwardly rotates the scapula during overhead reaching.

q: Which four muscles make up the rotator cuff?
o: Subscapularis, teres major, teres minor, coracobrachialis
e: Remember SITS. Teres major is not part of the cuff. All four run from the scapula to the humerus and stabilise the shoulder girdle.

q: Which rotator cuff muscle initiates abduction of the arm?
e: Supraspinatus accelerates abduction of the arm and decelerates adduction. It runs from the scapula, above the spine of the scapula, to the humerus.

q: Which rotator cuff muscle is the only one to internally rotate the shoulder?
e: Subscapularis sits on the anterior scapula and inserts on the anterior humerus, accelerating internal rotation. Infraspinatus and teres minor sit posteriorly and externally rotate.

q: Infraspinatus and teres minor share which action?
e: Both run from the scapula to the posterior humerus, accelerating external rotation and decelerating internal rotation while stabilising the shoulder girdle.

q: Teres major inserts where, and what does it do?
o: Anterior humerus; internal rotation, adduction and extension
e: Teres major runs from the scapula to the anterior humerus and mirrors latissimus dorsi, which is why it is nicknamed lat's little helper. It is not a rotator cuff muscle.

q: Which portion of the deltoid produces shoulder abduction?
e: Anterior deltoid accelerates shoulder flexion and internal rotation, lateral accelerates abduction, posterior accelerates extension and external rotation. All three run from the scapula and clavicle to the humerus.

q: Anterior and posterior deltoid are antagonists. Which pairing is correct?
o: Anterior flexes and internally rotates; posterior extends and externally rotates
Anterior extends and externally rotates; posterior flexes and internally rotates
e: Each decelerates what the other accelerates, which is why the posterior deltoid is the antagonist in a chest press and the anterior deltoid a synergist.

q: Where does pectoralis major originate?
e: It inserts on the anterior humerus and accelerates shoulder horizontal adduction and internal rotation, with the clavicular fibres also producing flexion.

q: Pectoralis major decelerates which movements?
o: Shoulder extension, horizontal abduction and external rotation
e: It decelerates the opposite of what it accelerates. In the upper-extremity distortion pattern it is the muscle stretched, because it is chronically shortened in rounded-shoulder posture.

q: What is pectoralis minor's action?
e: It protracts the scapulae and decelerates retraction. It is a secondary respiratory muscle in heavy or forced breathing, alongside the scalenes and sternocleidomastoid.

q: Serratus anterior originates on which structures?
e: From the upper nine ribs to the anterior scapula. It accelerates scapular protraction, decelerates retraction, and stabilises the scapulae against the rib cage.

q: The rhomboids accelerate which two scapular motions?
e: Rhomboid major and minor run from the thoracic spine to the scapula, retracting and downwardly rotating it, and decelerating protraction and upward rotation.

q: Which muscle accelerates scapular depression?
e: Lower trapezius depresses, middle retracts, upper elevates the scapula and extends, laterally flexes and rotates the neck. All three share the same broad origin and insertion.

q: Coracobrachialis runs from the scapula to the humerus. What does it do?
o: Flexes the humerus at the shoulder joint
e: From the A&P notes: origin scapula, insertion humerus, action flexion of the humerus at the shoulder joint. It also assists adduction.

q: Biceps brachii inserts on which bones?
e: It originates on the scapula and inserts on the radius and ulna, so it crosses the shoulder as well as the elbow.

q: Which three movements does biceps brachii accelerate?
o: Elbow flexion, supination of the radioulnar joint, shoulder flexion
Wrist flexion, elbow flexion, shoulder flexion
e: Elbow flexion, radioulnar supination and shoulder flexion. It decelerates elbow extension, pronation and shoulder extension, and stabilises the elbow and shoulder girdle.

q: Why is a supinated curl stronger than a pronated one?
o: The forearm is shorter when supinated
Biceps brachii is both an elbow flexor and a supinator, so supination puts it in its strongest position
The radius is thicker than the ulna
e: Pronation partially unwinds the biceps tendon on the radius and reduces its mechanical advantage, leaving more of the work to brachialis and brachioradialis.

q: Triceps brachii originates on which structures?
e: The long head arises from the scapula and the medial and lateral heads from the humerus. All insert on the ulna, at the olecranon.

q: Triceps brachii accelerates which two movements?
e: Because the long head crosses the shoulder, triceps extends the shoulder as well as the elbow, and decelerates elbow and shoulder flexion.

q: Brachialis differs from biceps brachii in that it:
o: Inserts on the ulna and so has no role in supination
e: From the humerus to the ulna. Because the ulna does not rotate, brachialis is a pure elbow flexor regardless of forearm position.

q: Brachioradialis runs from the humerus to which bone?
e: Humerus to radius, accelerating elbow flexion and decelerating elbow extension. It is strongest with the forearm in a neutral, thumbs-up position, as in a hammer curl.

q: Anconeus, from the humerus to the ulna, does what?
e: From the A&P notes: a small muscle assisting triceps in elbow extension.

q: Pronator teres runs from the medial humerus and ulna to the radius. What does it do?
o: Pronates the forearm at the elbow joint
e: Pronation turns the palm from up to down. Its antagonist, supinator radii brevis, runs from the lateral humerus and ulna to the radius and supinates.

q: Which muscle supinates the forearm at the elbow joint, from the lateral humerus and ulna?
e: Supinator radii brevis inserts on the radius. Biceps brachii is the other, more powerful, supinator, but only when the elbow is flexed.

q: Flexor carpi radialis originates on the medial humerus. What is its action?
o: Flexes and abducts the hand at the wrist
Flexes and adducts the hand at the wrist
e: Radialis means thumb side, so it flexes and abducts. Flexor carpi ulnaris, on the little-finger side, flexes and adducts.

q: Flexor carpi ulnaris flexes and does what else at the wrist?
e: Ulnaris means little-finger side, so its pull adducts the hand. It runs from the medial humerus to the metacarpals.

q: Where do the wrist flexors originate as a group?
e: The flexors arise from the medial humerus, at the medial epicondyle, and the extensors from the lateral humerus, at the lateral epicondyle. That is the anatomy behind golfer's and tennis elbow respectively.

q: Extensor carpi radialis extends and:
o: Adducts the hand at the wrist
Abducts the hand at the wrist
e: Radialis, thumb side, so abduction. Extensor carpi ulnaris extends and adducts. Both originate on the lateral humerus and insert on a metacarpal.

q: Flexor carpi digitorum inserts on the phalanges. What does it do?
o: Flexes the hand at the wrist and the finger joints
e: Because it crosses the wrist and continues to the phalanges it acts on both. Extensor carpi digitorum is its mirror, extending the hand at the wrist and extending the fingers.

q: The thenar eminence is the muscle mass on which side of the palm, and what does it do?
o: Little finger side; abduction and flexion of the little finger
Thumb side; adduction, abduction and flexion of the thumb
Centre of the palm; finger flexion
Back of the hand; finger extension
e: Thenar is the thumb side, hypothenar the little finger side. The hypothenar eminence abducts and flexes the little finger.

q: Sternocleidomastoid runs from the sternum and clavicle to which landmark?
o: The mastoid process on the temporal bone
e: The name itself gives the attachments. It accelerates cervical flexion, rotation and lateral flexion, and stabilises the cervical spine and acromioclavicular joint.

q: Besides moving the neck, what do the scalenes do?
e: They are secondary respiratory muscles, recruited in heavy or forced breathing alongside sternocleidomastoid and pectoralis minor. They also flex, rotate and laterally flex the cervical spine.

q: Splenius capitis runs from the vertebrae to the occiput. What happens when only one side contracts?
o: The head laterally flexes to the opposite side
e: From the A&P notes: one side rotates the head, both sides extend it.

q: Longus colli and longus capitis are deep anterior neck muscles. What do they accelerate?
e: Longus colli produces cervical flexion, lateral flexion and ipsilateral rotation; longus capitis produces cervical flexion and lateral flexion. Both stabilise the cervical spine, and both are typically weak in forward-head posture.

q: Extensor digitorum longus, from the tibia and fibula to the phalanges, does what?
o: Dorsiflexes the foot and extends the four lateral toes
e: From the A&P notes. Its counterpart, flexor digitorum longus, runs from the tibia to the phalanges and flexes the lateral four toes.

q: Which muscle flexes the lateral four toes?
e: Flexor digitorum longus runs from the tibia to the phalanges. Together with tibialis posterior it contributes to arch support and toe-off.

q: In the NASM muscle tables, what does 'accelerates' mean?
o: The concentric action the muscle produces
The isometric hold the muscle provides
e: Accelerates is the concentric action, decelerates the eccentric action it controls, and stabilises the isometric role. Each muscle is described in all three.

q: Gluteus maximus accelerates hip extension and external rotation. What does it decelerate?
o: Hip flexion and internal rotation, plus tibial internal rotation via the iliotibial band
e: It decelerates the opposite of what it accelerates, and its iliotibial band attachment gives it influence on the tibia as well. It stabilises the LPHC.

q: Which structure does the psoas stabilise, and what does it rotate?
e: Psoas runs from the lumbar spine to the femur, accelerating hip flexion and external rotation and rotating the lumbar spine, while stabilising the LPHC. Iliacus shares the hip actions but not the spinal one.

q: Which two hip muscles differ mainly in that one attaches to the spine and one to the ilium?
e: Psoas originates on the lumbar spine, iliacus on the iliac bones. Both insert on the femur and accelerate hip flexion and external rotation, but only psoas can rotate the lumbar spine.

q: Gluteus medius has different actions in its anterior and posterior fibres. Which is correct?
o: Anterior abduct and externally rotate; posterior abduct and internally rotate
Anterior abduct and internally rotate; posterior abduct and externally rotate
e: Anterior fibres accelerate abduction and internal rotation; posterior fibres accelerate abduction and external rotation. Gluteus minimus abducts and internally rotates.

q: Adductor magnus is listed twice in the NASM table. Why?
o: Its anterior fibres flex and internally rotate the hip while its posterior fibres extend and externally rotate it
It is both an adductor and an abductor
e: Both sets adduct, but the anterior fibres accelerate hip flexion and internal rotation and the posterior fibres accelerate hip extension and external rotation.

q: Tensor fasciae latae accelerates which three movements?
o: Knee flexion, hip abduction, internal rotation
e: From the ilium via the iliotibial tract to the tibia. It decelerates hip extension, adduction and external rotation, and stabilises the LPHC.

q: Semitendinosus accelerates knee flexion, hip extension and which rotation?
e: Medial hamstrings internally rotate the tibia. It runs from the ischial tuberosity to the tibia and stabilises the LPHC and knee.

q: Rectus femoris is listed as stabilising which two regions?
e: Because it crosses both hip and knee, running from the iliac bone to the tibia via the patella, it accelerates knee extension and hip flexion. The three vasti stabilise only the knee.

q: Which muscle accelerates ipsilateral elevation of the pelvis?
e: QL runs from the iliac crest to the twelfth rib and lumbar vertebrae, accelerating ipsilateral lateral flexion and hip hiking, and fixing the twelfth rib to stabilise the diaphragm's attachments during inspiration.

q: Transverse abdominis is listed with no deceleration action. What does it accelerate instead?
o: An increase in intra-abdominal pressure, supporting the abdominal viscera
e: It runs from the iliac crest, inguinal ligament, lumbar fascia and lower ribs to the linea alba, and its job is pressure and stability rather than movement. It stabilises the LPHC.

q: External oblique produces rotation to which side?
e: External oblique accelerates contralateral rotation, internal oblique ipsilateral rotation. Both also flex and laterally flex the spine and stabilise the LPHC.

q: Multifidus accelerates spinal extension and which rotation?
e: Spinal extension and contralateral rotation, decelerating spinal flexion and rotation. It stabilises the spine segment by segment.

q: Latissimus dorsi decelerates shoulder flexion, abduction, external rotation and what else?
e: Because it attaches to the thoracic and lumbar spine and iliac crest, it also decelerates spinal flexion. It stabilises the LPHC and shoulder, linking the arm to the pelvis.

q: Levator scapulae, with the scapulae anchored, accelerates which neck movements?
o: Cervical extension, lateral flexion and ipsilateral rotation
e: With the neck stabilised instead, it assists scapular elevation and downward rotation. Which end is fixed determines which end moves.

q: A client's knees buckle inward during a squat. Which muscles are overactive and which underactive?
o: Overactive adductors, underactive gluteus medius and minimus
e: The adductor complex pulls the femur into adduction and internal rotation; the outer hip fails to resist it. Release and stretch the adductors, strengthen the outer hip.

q: In a push-up, what is the role of the rotator cuff?
e: It holds the humeral head centred in the glenoid while pectoralis major, anterior deltoid and triceps do the moving. That is the stabiliser role in NASM's terms.

q: Which muscle pair are the two ends of the same lever in anterior pelvic tilt?
e: A short psoas pulls the lumbar spine and pelvis forward; a weak gluteus maximus fails to pull it back. Tight hip flexors and weak glutes are not two findings but two ends of one lever.

q: Why does a pull-up recruit both latissimus dorsi and biceps brachii?
o: Latissimus dorsi extends and adducts the shoulder as agonist, while biceps brachii flexes the elbow as synergist
e: Two joints move at once, so two muscle groups contribute. NASM lists the biceps as a synergist assisting the latissimus dorsi in a pull-up.

q: During the lowering phase of a biceps curl, what is the biceps doing?
o: Contracting eccentrically to decelerate elbow extension
e: The muscle exerts less force than the load, so it lengthens under control. That is exactly what the NASM tables mean by decelerating elbow extension.

q: Which muscles must lengthen for full overhead reaching, and which must work?
o: Lengthen the rhomboids and lower trapezius; work the pectorals
Lengthen the pectorals and latissimus dorsi; work serratus anterior and upper and lower trapezius for upward rotation
Lengthen the deltoid; work the biceps
Lengthen the triceps; work the rhomboids
e: Overhead reaching needs scapular upward rotation, produced by serratus anterior with upper and lower trapezius, and it is blocked by tight pectorals and latissimus dorsi. That is why arms fall forward in the overhead squat.

q: Which single muscle would you suspect first if a client cannot hold a level pelvis in single-leg stance?
e: Gluteus medius is the primary frontal-plane pelvic stabiliser. Its weakness shows as the opposite hip dropping and often as knee valgus further down the chain.

q: A muscle crossing two joints can be limited by active insufficiency. Which is an example?
o: Soleus during a seated calf raise
Hamstrings trying to flex the knee fully while the hip is already extended
e: Shortened at both ends, a two-joint muscle cannot generate full force. The same principle explains why rectus femoris is a weaker knee extensor when the hip is flexed.

q: Which muscles are the primary movers in a standing calf raise with the knee straight?
e: Gastrocnemius crosses the knee, so it is at better length with the knee straight. Bending the knee shortens it and shifts the work to soleus.

q: Which muscle group would you strengthen to reduce excessive pronation at the foot?
o: Tibialis posterior and tibialis anterior, the invertors
e: The invertors resist the arch collapsing. In the lower-extremity distortion pattern the calves and adductors are stretched and the foot and ankle stabilisers, notably anterior tibialis, are strengthened.

q: Which muscle inserts on the lesser trochanter of the femur?
e: Psoas major and iliacus share that insertion. Gluteus medius, minimus and piriformis all insert on the greater trochanter; the adductors insert on the linea aspera.

q: Which muscles insert on the greater trochanter?
o: Gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and piriformis
e: The abductors and the deep external rotators converge on the greater trochanter, the lateral bony prominence at the top of the femur.

q: Which muscles originate on the ischial tuberosity?
o: The hamstrings, plus the posterior fibres of adductor magnus
e: Biceps femoris long head, semitendinosus and semimembranosus all arise there, which is why sitting bone pain often traces back to hamstring attachment. The short head of biceps femoris is the exception, arising from the linea aspera.

q: Which three muscles insert together at the pes anserinus on the medial tibia?
e: Say goodbye to my grandmother: Sartorius, Gracilis, semiTendinosus. Three muscles from three different groups, sharing one insertion.

q: Which muscle inserts on the anterior humerus and originates on the thoracic and lumbar spine and iliac crest?
e: Latissimus dorsi. Its span from the pelvis to the arm is why it links shoulder motion to the LPHC and why it decelerates spinal flexion as well as shoulder flexion.

q: Which muscles insert on the medial border of the scapula?
o: Rhomboid major, rhomboid minor and serratus anterior
e: The rhomboids pull it medially from the spine, serratus anterior pulls it laterally from the ribs. They are direct antagonists across the same border.

q: Which muscle originates on the sacrum and inserts on the femur?
e: Piriformis runs from the anterior sacrum to the greater trochanter. Gluteus maximus also has a sacral origin, but it arises from the innominate bone, sacrum and coccyx together.

q: Which muscle originates on the iliac bone and inserts on the tibia via the patella?
e: Rectus femoris is the only quadriceps with a pelvic origin, so it is the only one that flexes the hip. The three vasti arise from the femur itself.

q: Which muscle attaches the sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process?
e: The name lists the attachments in order: sterno, cleido (clavicle), mastoid.

q: Which muscle runs from the pubis to the ribs and sternum?
e: That vertical line of pull produces spinal flexion. External oblique runs the other way, from the lower ribs down to the iliac crest and linea alba.

q: Which muscle originates on the iliac crest and inserts on the twelfth rib and lumbar vertebrae?
e: QL. Besides lateral flexion and hip hiking, it fixes the twelfth rib to stabilise the diaphragm's attachments during inspiration.

q: Besides piriformis, which muscles make up the deep external rotators of the hip?
o: Obturator internus and externus, superior and inferior gemellus, and quadratus femoris
e: Six small muscles running from the pelvis to the greater trochanter. They externally rotate the hip and, importantly, provide fine control of femoral rotation during gait.

q: Why does piriformis change its action when the hip is flexed past about 90 degrees?
o: Its line of pull relative to the joint axis changes, so it abducts rather than externally rotating
e: Line of pull, not the muscle, determines the action. This is the same principle behind role switching, where one muscle acts as agonist, synergist or stabiliser depending on the position.

q: Where does semimembranosus insert?
o: Posterior aspect of the medial tibial condyle
Pes anserinus on the medial tibia
e: Semimembranosus goes to the posterior medial tibial condyle, semitendinosus to the pes anserinus. Both are medial hamstrings and both internally rotate the flexed knee.

q: Which hamstring has two heads, and where does each arise?
o: Biceps femoris; long head from the ischial tuberosity, short head from the linea aspera
e: Only the long head crosses the hip. The short head crosses the knee alone, which is why it flexes the knee but does not extend the hip.

q: Which quadriceps lies deepest, directly on the femur beneath rectus femoris?
e: Vastus intermedius sits under rectus femoris on the anterior femur. Like the other vasti it originates on the femur, inserts on the tibia via the patella, and only extends the knee.

q: Which small muscle sits between gastrocnemius and soleus and is often absent?
e: Plantaris has a small belly and a very long thin tendon. It weakly assists plantar flexion and knee flexion and is functionally minor.

q: Together, gastrocnemius and soleus are known as:
e: Three muscle bellies, two heads of gastrocnemius plus soleus, sharing the Achilles tendon into the calcaneus.

q: Which erector spinae column lies closest to the spinous processes?
e: From lateral to medial: iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis. Iliocostalis attaches out toward the ribs, hence the name.

q: Unilateral contraction of erector spinae produces which movements?
o: Lateral flexion and rotation to the same side
e: Bilaterally they extend the spine; unilaterally they laterally flex and rotate. They decelerate spinal flexion, rotation and lateral flexion and stabilise the spine during functional movement.

q: What do the external intercostals do?
e: With the diaphragm they are the primary muscles of quiet inspiration. Internal intercostals depress the ribs and contribute to forced expiration.

q: Which muscles are recruited only in heavy or forced inspiration?
e: They are the secondary respiratory muscles. Visible contraction of the neck muscles at rest is a sign of the abnormal upper-chest breathing pattern that warrants referral.

q: Which muscles produce active, forced expiration?
o: The abdominal muscles and internal intercostals compressing the thoracic cavity
e: Quiet expiration is passive, from relaxation of the inspiratory muscles. Forced expiration needs muscles that actively squeeze the cavity.

q: Where does supraspinatus sit on the scapula?
o: Below the spine of the scapula
In the fossa above the spine of the scapula
e: Supra means above. Infraspinatus sits below the spine of the scapula, subscapularis on the anterior, costal surface, and teres minor along the lateral border.

q: Which rotator cuff muscle sits on the anterior surface of the scapula?
e: Sub-scapular means under the scapula. Its anterior position is exactly why it is the internal rotator of the group.

q: Which muscle would you suspect in a client whose scapula wings away from the rib cage?
e: Serratus anterior holds the medial border flat against the ribs. Weakness lets the border lift, and it also impairs the scapular upward rotation needed for overhead reaching.

q: Scapular upward rotation, needed to reach overhead, is produced by:
o: Upper trapezius, lower trapezius and serratus anterior working as a force couple
e: Three muscles pulling in different directions produce one rotation. The rhomboids and levator scapulae do the opposite, downward rotation.

q: Which two muscles are the main scapular downward rotators?
e: Both accelerate retraction or elevation with downward rotation, and both decelerate the upward rotation produced by serratus anterior and trapezius.

q: Which portion of trapezius extends, laterally flexes and rotates the cervical spine as well as elevating the scapula?
o: None; trapezius does not act on the neck
e: Upper trapezius shares an origin with the rest of the muscle along the cervical and thoracic spine and clavicle, but its fibres reach the occipital bone, so it moves the head as well.

q: Which head of triceps brachii crosses the shoulder joint?
e: The long head arises from the scapula, the other two from the humerus. That is why triceps extends the shoulder as well as the elbow.

q: Which three muscles flex the elbow, and which is strongest in a neutral grip?
o: Biceps, brachialis, brachioradialis; brachioradialis is strongest neutral
Biceps, triceps, anconeus; biceps strongest neutral
Brachialis, supinator, pronator teres; supinator strongest
Biceps, coracobrachialis, brachialis; biceps strongest neutral
e: Biceps is strongest supinated, brachialis works in any position because it inserts on the non-rotating ulna, and brachioradialis is best placed in the neutral, hammer-curl grip.

q: Which muscles are the agonists in a squat, in NASM's table?
e: Agonists gluteus maximus and quadriceps, synergist hamstrings, stabiliser transversus abdominis, antagonist psoas.

q: NASM lists the muscle synergies of an overhead press as:
e: From Table 2.5. A cable row pairs latissimus dorsi, rhomboids and posterior deltoid; a chest press pairs pectoralis major, anterior deltoid and triceps brachii.

q: In a cable row, which three muscles work as a synergy?
o: Latissimus dorsi, rhomboids and posterior deltoid
Pectoralis major, anterior deltoid and triceps
e: All three pull the arm and scapula backward. NASM separately lists latissimus dorsi as the agonist in a row, posterior deltoid and biceps as synergists, rotator cuff as stabiliser and pectoralis major as antagonist.

q: A client's arms fall forward in the overhead squat. Which muscles get flexibility work?
o: Pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, latissimus dorsi and upper trapezius
e: Overactivity across the front of the shoulder and the lat pulls the arms down and forward. The underactive side, the middle and lower trapezius, rhomboids and rotator cuff, gets activation and strengthening.

q: Which two muscles are most implicated in the LPHC distortion pattern's stretch list?
o: Psoas and rectus femoris, the hip flexors
e: Both cross the front of the hip and shorten with sitting. Their opposites, the gluteals and deep core, are the ones strengthened.

q: Why can weakness of gluteus maximus show up as low back pain?
o: It attaches to the lumbar vertebrae
When it fails to extend the hip, the erector spinae and hamstrings compensate and the pelvis tilts anteriorly, loading the lumbar spine
It shares a nerve with the spine
e: The lumbar spine carries the most weight and the largest forces already. Compensation by muscles not designed for the job increases that load.

q: Which muscle acts on the tibia through the iliotibial band despite never touching it directly at the hip?
e: NASM lists gluteus maximus as decelerating tibial internal rotation via the iliotibial band, because part of its insertion is into the band rather than the femur.

q: Which two muscles both insert into the iliotibial band?
o: Gluteus maximus and tensor fasciae latae
e: One from behind, one from in front, so the band is tensioned from both directions. That is why lateral knee pain often traces back to the hip rather than the knee.

q: During the lowering phase of a squat, what are the quadriceps doing?
o: Contracting concentrically to produce knee flexion
Contracting eccentrically to decelerate knee flexion
e: Gravity produces the flexion; the quadriceps control the rate of it. In the NASM tables this is exactly what decelerates knee flexion means.

q: Which muscles decelerate hip adduction during single-leg landing?
e: They contract eccentrically to stop the femur collapsing inward. Failure of this is the mechanism behind knee valgus on landing.

q: Which muscle group must lengthen for full hip extension in a lunge or a bridge?
o: The hip flexors, notably psoas and rectus femoris
e: They are the antagonists to hip extension. If they cannot lengthen, the pelvis tips anteriorly and the lumbar spine extends to fake the range.

q: Which muscle pairing is the classic antagonist relationship at the ankle?
o: Tibialis anterior against gastrocnemius and soleus
e: Dorsiflexion against plantar flexion in the sagittal plane. In the frontal plane the pairing is the invertors, tibialis anterior and posterior, against the evertors, the peroneals.

q: Limited ankle dorsiflexion often shows up in an overhead squat as:
o: Excessive forward lean, because the shin cannot travel forward over the foot
e: The ideal is a parallel line between shin and torso. If the shin cannot come forward, the torso must lean instead to keep the centre of mass over the feet.

q: Which muscles most directly oppose one another in producing pelvic tilt?
o: Rectus abdominis and gluteals against hip flexors and erector spinae
e: Posterior tilters are the abdominals and gluteals; anterior tilters are the hip flexors and erector spinae. Anterior pelvic tilt is the second pair winning.

q: Which nerve root level is most associated with the muscles of the lower limb, arising from which plexus?
e: The lumbosacral plexus supplies the lower limb; the brachial plexus supplies the upper limb. Recall the peripheral nervous system as 12 cranial nerves, 31 pairs of spinal nerves and sensory receptors.

q: Where are muscle spindles located relative to the muscle fibres?
e: Parallel, which is what lets them sense change in muscle length and its rate. Golgi tendon organs sit where the fibres insert into the tendon and sense tension instead.

q: Which receptor makes a held static stretch possible?
o: The muscle spindle, which resists it
The Golgi tendon organ, whose activation causes the muscle to relax
e: The spindle fires first and resists a fast stretch; sustained tension activates the GTO, which relaxes the muscle. That is the physiology behind holding a stretch rather than bouncing.

q: Which connective tissue layer wraps a single fascicle?
e: Epimysium wraps the whole muscle, perimysium each fascicle, endomysium the individual fibres. All three converge at the ends to form the tendon.

q: What is a fascicle?
o: The largest bundles of fibres within a muscle
The plasma membrane of a fibre
A repeating unit of actin and myosin
e: Muscle to fascicle to fibre to myofibril to myofilament. Each level has its own connective tissue wrapping.

q: Which structure transmits muscular force to bone?
e: Tendons attach muscle to bone and provide the anchor from which the muscle exerts force. Ligaments attach bone to bone. Both have poor vascularity.

q: Why can a group like the four quadriceps act as a functional unit?
o: Connective tissue links them and transmits their forces together to the bone
e: Connective tissue lets muscles work as functional groups, which is why the four quadriceps together extend the knee despite having different origins.

q: Which is the correct agonist for shoulder flexion?
e: NASM lists anterior deltoid as the prime mover for shoulder flexion, with the clavicular fibres of pectoralis major assisting. The antagonists are the posterior deltoid and latissimus dorsi.

q: Which is the agonist for elbow extension, and which its antagonist?
e: They swap roles on the return: in elbow flexion the biceps is agonist and the triceps antagonist. Roles depend on the joint motion of the moment, not on the muscle.

q: Which muscle is the agonist for knee extension?
e: The quadriceps as a group. The hamstrings are the antagonists at the knee, though both groups work together at the hip during a squat.

q: Why do the hamstrings act as both agonist and antagonist during a squat?
o: They extend the hip as synergist while opposing knee extension as antagonist at the other joint
e: A two-joint muscle can play different roles at each joint at the same time. This is why NASM insists a muscle's role depends on the joint motion happening at that moment.

q: Which muscles would you strengthen for a client with a forward head posture?
o: The deep cervical flexors, longus colli and longus capitis, plus the middle and lower trapezius
e: The deep front of the neck is lengthened and weak; the upper trapezius, levator scapulae and sternocleidomastoid are short and overactive and get flexibility work instead.

q: Which muscle is the prime mover in a pull-up?
e: Latissimus dorsi extends and adducts the shoulder, which is the movement of pulling the body up. The biceps assist at the elbow as synergists.

q: Transversus abdominis and multifidus are often trained together. Why?
o: They are the deep local stabilisers of the spine, one producing pressure and one controlling intersegmental motion
e: Neither produces much visible movement. Their job is stability, which is why the LPHC corrective approach strengthens the core alongside the gluteals.

q: Which muscle group is stretched and which strengthened in the lower-extremity distortion pattern?
o: Stretch the gluteals and anterior tibialis; strengthen the calves
Stretch the calves and adductor complex; strengthen the foot and ankle stabilisers and the gluteals
Stretch the hamstrings; strengthen the quadriceps
Stretch the peroneals; strengthen the adductors
e: Flat feet with knock knees. What is held short, the calves and inner thighs, gets flexibility; what is held long, the anterior tibialis and gluteals, gets strengthening.

q: A client cannot keep their heels down in a squat. Which muscles are most likely restricted?
e: They plantarflex, so shortness limits dorsiflexion and lifts the heel. Note that gastrocnemius is affected by knee angle and soleus is not, which can help distinguish them.

q: Which muscle is both a hip flexor and a knee flexor?
e: Sartorius flexes, abducts and externally rotates the hip while flexing and internally rotating the knee. Rectus femoris is the opposite combination, a hip flexor and a knee extensor.

q: Which muscle would you expect to be short in a client who sits all day and reports a tight lower back?
e: Sitting holds it shortened, and it originates on the lumbar spine, so standing pulls the lumbar spine forward. Tight hip flexors and weak glutes are two ends of the same lever.

q: Which muscle accelerates hip flexion and external rotation while also rotating the lumbar spine?
e: Only psoas has a spinal attachment, so only psoas rotates the lumbar spine. Iliacus shares the hip actions but arises on the iliac bones.

q: Which muscle accelerates hip abduction and internal rotation and decelerates hip adduction and external rotation?
e: Gluteus minimus, and the anterior fibres of gluteus medius do the same. The posterior fibres of medius reverse the rotation component.

q: Which muscle accelerates scapular protraction?
e: Both pull the scapula forward around the rib cage. Both decelerate retraction, which the rhomboids and middle trapezius produce.

q: Which muscle decelerates shoulder external rotation?
e: Subscapularis accelerates internal rotation and therefore decelerates external rotation. Infraspinatus and teres minor do the reverse.

q: Which muscle accelerates shoulder horizontal adduction?
e: Pectoralis major, with the anterior deltoid assisting. That is the movement of a chest fly, and the posterior deltoid decelerates it.

q: Which muscle accelerates knee flexion, hip extension and tibial internal rotation?
e: A medial hamstring, so the rotation is internal. Biceps femoris shares the flexion and extension but rotates the tibia externally.

q: Which muscle increases intra-abdominal pressure and supports the abdominal viscera?
e: It is listed with no deceleration action in the NASM tables, because it stabilises rather than moves. Its fibres run horizontally like a corset.

q: Which muscle pulls the central tendon inferiorly, increasing thoracic cavity volume?
e: That is the mechanism of inspiration: increasing volume lowers intrapulmonary pressure below atmospheric, so air is drawn in.

q: Which muscle accelerates cervical flexion, rotation and lateral flexion, and stabilises the acromioclavicular joint?
e: Its clavicular attachment is why it is credited with stabilising the acromioclavicular joint as well as the cervical spine.

q: Which muscle accelerates scapular retraction without downward rotation?
e: Middle trapezius purely retracts and decelerates protraction. The rhomboids retract and downwardly rotate at the same time.

q: Teres major and latissimus dorsi share which three actions?
e: Both run to the anterior humerus and pull it back, in and inward. Teres major differs only in arising from the scapula rather than the spine and pelvis.

q: Which muscle decelerates hip abduction, extension and external rotation?
e: Adductor longus, brevis, the anterior fibres of magnus, gracilis and pectineus all accelerate hip adduction, flexion and internal rotation, so they decelerate the opposite.

q: Which is the best single description of a synergist?
o: The muscle most responsible for the movement
A muscle creating force to assist the prime mover without being the primary producer
A muscle contracting isometrically to hold a joint
A muscle performing the opposite action
e: Examples: hamstrings with gluteus maximus in hip extension, triceps assisting pectorals in a chest press, biceps assisting latissimus dorsi in a pull-up.

q: Why does NASM describe every muscle as accelerating, decelerating and stabilising?
o: Because muscles work across the whole action spectrum: concentric, eccentric and isometric
Because each muscle has three parts
e: Traditional training emphasises the concentric only. Describing all three reflects that the entire spectrum should be trained to maximise strength, maintain range of motion and prevent injury.

q: Which muscle is described as stabilising the sacroiliac joints?
e: Piriformis runs directly across the back of the sacroiliac joint from the sacrum to the femur, so its tension affects that joint directly.

q: Which muscles cross both the hip and the knee?
o: Rectus femoris, the hamstrings except the short head of biceps femoris, sartorius, gracilis and TFL via the iliotibial band
e: Two-joint muscles at the hip and knee are the ones most subject to active and passive insufficiency, and the ones whose tightness shows up as compensation in a squat.

q: Why do the gastrocnemius and hamstrings both influence the knee in a straight-leg forward bend?
o: Both cross the knee, so shortness in either limits the movement
e: The hamstrings cross the hip and knee, gastrocnemius crosses the knee and ankle. A straight-leg bend loads both chains at once.

q: Which muscle would you target to improve toe-off in walking?
o: Gastrocnemius and soleus, with flexor hallucis and digitorum longus
e: Toe-off is plantar flexion combined with supination for force production. Tibialis anterior does the opposite job, clearing the foot during the swing phase.

q: Which muscle group controls the foot during the force-reduction phase of gait?
o: The invertors and the intrinsic foot muscles, eccentrically controlling pronation
e: Pronation happens during force reduction and must be controlled rather than prevented. Tibialis posterior and anterior are the main eccentric brakes on it.

q: A client has weak rhomboids and a tight pectoralis minor. What would you expect to see?
o: Protracted, downwardly rotated scapulae and rounded shoulders
e: Pectoralis minor protracts and tips the scapula forward; the rhomboids fail to hold it back. That is the scapular half of the upper-extremity distortion pattern.

q: Which muscle is most responsible for hip hiking on one side?
e: QL accelerates ipsilateral elevation of the pelvis. Unilateral tightness produces a hip hike and a functional leg-length difference.

q: Which muscle would you suspect if a client cannot maintain a neutral spine during a plank and their lower back sags?
o: Transversus abdominis and rectus abdominis failing to resist extension
e: A plank is an isometric anti-extension task. The abdominal wall must hold the pelvis and spine against gravity pulling them into extension.

q: Which single principle explains why the same muscle can be agonist in one exercise and antagonist in another?
o: A muscle's role depends on the joint motion happening at the moment
e: The infraspinatus is the standard example: agonist for shoulder external rotation, synergist when the shoulder reaches overhead, stabiliser during other shoulder motions.
